newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agents resume search at clinic blast site.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agents resume search at clinic blast site.

text.p: Federal agents swarmed through wreckage left by two bomb blasts at an Atlanta abortion clinic on Friday, searching for clues to an attack that injured at least half a dozen people.

Police maintained a cordon in a 100-yard (metre) radius around the building in the Atlanta suburb of Sandy Springs, stopping workers hoping to return to their jobs and media who attempted to retrieve equipment left behind in panic when a second explosion occurred on Thursday.

Investigators stopped searching for additional devices and instead were concentrating on finding clues in the two blasts, said Robert Browning, an agent with the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms.
"The area has been determined to be clear," he said.

The bombings, about an hour apart, rocked a building housing the Atlanta Northside Family Planning Services centre -- the same clinic that was the target of Atlanta's last abortion clinic bombing 13 years ago.

The first bomb exploded about 9:30 a.m. EST (1430 GMT). An hour later, as law enforcement officials and local firefighters sifted through debris, a second bomb detonated near a garbage container in the building's parking lot, injuring six people including agents from the FBI and ATF.
Police said there was no warning of the attack and no one claimed responsibility.
The second explosion left investigators wondering if the initial device had been a so-called sucker bomb intended to lure police and other emergency workers to the area.
Police stopped residents and workers near the clinic during the Friday morning rush hour, asking if they had seen anything suspicious the previous morning.
"Right now, we've got more Feds around here than you can shake a stick at," said Ron Knapp, an insurance claims investigator. "Anybody who tries anything here today has got to be pretty stupid."

Some workers in the building housing the clinic tried to get in but were turned away by federal agents. "We just came to get our car today, but they haven't freed up the crime scene yet," said Patricia Pittler, who works in a first-floor dentist office.

NBC affiliate WXIA-TV reported federal agents scrutinised the television station's aerial footage of the scene and believed the second bomb had been placed not in the garbage container but in nearby bushes at the base of a telephone pole.

If correct, the report concluded, emergency workers and news reporters who had congregated nearby may have been spared serious injury by two parked cars, one of which belonged to Fulton County Police Chief Louis Graham.

The clinic sees patients only on certain days and Thursday was not one of them, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Just three people were in the clinic when the first bomb went off. On a clinic day there might have been 15-20 employees as well as patients, the newspaper said.
A clinic worker said the operating room, waiting room and counselling room were ruined.
None of the injuries was considered critical. An FBI agent injured in the bombing remained in a local hospital on Friday, suffering from a bruise to his brain.

Although the abortion clinic appeared to be the target of the attack, officials said they could not rule out the possibility that the bombing was directed at other offices in the building, which also housed a drug rehabilitation clinic and a law office specialising in divorce.
Federal investigators also were checking for any links to last July's Centennial Olympic Park bombing in downtown Atlanta, which left two people dead and more than 100 injured.
Authorities also sought clues from the general public, inviting calls to a toll-free ATF hotline: (888) ATF-BOMB.
Anti-abortion activists attacked three abortion clinics in the Atlanta area in 1984, including the Atlanta Northside centre, but no one was ever prosecuted.
